CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Drama — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the drama club habit: a warm-up body, a borrowed character, and the discovery that speaking in someone else’s voice is the easiest way to find your own.

What is this?

Drama club is pretend with structure — characters, voices, and small stories performed for anyone in the room. The card’s printed skills are Stories & Confidence: inventing the tale and standing up while telling it.

What does it mean?

Playing a character lets a shy child say bold things safely — the dragon says what the child is not ready to. Inventing stories trains sequencing (first, then, suddenly) which is the skeleton of every school essay later.

What does the child need to know?

A corner that can be a stage, three random objects as story props, and an audience of one or more. Costumes are optional; a hat changes everything.

Why this matters

Drama builds language, sequencing, empathy (every character has feelings to manage) and the specific courage of being watched. It is the club where shy children regularly become loud ones.

What it teaches

Story sequencing, voice control, emotional vocabulary, eye contact with an audience, improvisation (a story that bends when a prop changes), and stage courage.

Words to learn

characterscenestageaudiencecostumeactbowvoicestory

Say this to your child

“"Drama club is open! Warm up your walking... now pick your character — who are you today? Give them a voice. Here are three mystery props: the story must use all three!"”

Step by step

  1. Warm up the body: walk like a robot, glide like a cat, stomp like a giant.
  2. Pick the character: name, voice, and the walk that goes with it.
  3. Open the story suitcase — three objects — and build the story around them.
  4. Perform the one-scene show for the audience; the audience claps between scenes.
  5. Take the bow together — performers and audience — then swap roles so every actor gets a turn and every audience gets a turn too.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the actor gestures with an open hand mid-story — the gesture is doing the words’ job, which is exactly what actors mean by showing, not telling.

Ask your child

"What is your character’s name?" "How does your character feel right now?" "What happens when the spoon arrives in the story?" "How does an actor end the show?" (with a bow)

What your child can say or do

Your child may stay in character through dinner, give the audience speaking roles, or discover the microphone-power of the hairbrush — every theater has one.

Out in the real world

Actors, teachers, lawyers and YouTubers all live on this skill: standing in front of people and carrying a story. The living-room stage is the first one.

Try it together

The interview show: one player is a celebrity (a cat, an astronaut, a pancake chef), the other is the reporter with five questions. Switch roles after the commercials.

Understanding check

Ask: "What three things does a character need?" (a name, a voice, a walk) "What do we do with the story suitcase?" (use all three props) "How do we end a show?" (bow together)

This lesson pairs with the Drama flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
